utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, would you call your next witness, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour, I call Rajko Karanovic. RAJKO KARANOVIC, called

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Sir, would you please take the oath that has been given you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I shall speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you. You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Sir, is your name Rajko Karanovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Do you live in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Do you originate from Prijedor or from elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was born at Novi Grad and I have lived in Prijedor for the past 25 years.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: How old are you, Mr. Karanovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 40 years old.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Do you live in Prijedor with your family, your wife and children?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Were you mobilized in May 1992 before the conflict in Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can you remember what date that was that you were mobilized?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: When would that have been?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On 22nd May 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: When did your mobilization finish?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On 9th February 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you know Dusko Tadic before the conflict in Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you know of the Tadic family before the conflict in Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I only heard the name.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: In what connection did you hear the name Tadic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I went to Kozara Mountain and I used to come to his coffee shop, the coffee shop belonging to the Tadic family. I heard that that was their coffee shop.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you take part in the conflict in Kozarac at the end of May 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was delivering food for the army, for the troops in Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: When did you start that duty of delivering food to the army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was on 28th May, roughly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: From where did you receive your orders to deliver food? What Unit were you part of?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was the 43rd Motorized Brigade in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your role of delivering food, did that put you within the catering section of the army, or in the transport section?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was part of the transport section.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you deliver food to the army in Kozarac by bringing supplies from Prijedor and delivering them to Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Do you know Dusko Tadic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: When did you come to know Dusko Tadic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In June of the year 1992 I met him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Whereabouts did you meet him for the first time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the police checkpoint between Prijedor and Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Does that checkpoint have a name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The police checkpoint.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Is it at a particular place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: What is the name of that place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Orlovci.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can you recollect for how long you saw Dusko Tadic at checkpoint Orlovci?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In June and July, part of July, some 40 days.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Why were you passing through checkpoint Orlovci?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because this was the only way to reach Kozarac from Prijedor. So that was actually my route and that was usual, regular route that I took.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: How many times a day did you take this route?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Three, sometimes even four times a day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Were those supplies that you were taking at breakfast time, lunch time and supper time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right, exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you deliver any supplies to any soldiers or police who were on duty at checkpoint Orlovci?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, this was not my duty. I had no obligation towards them, but I used to give them food.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: When you saw Dusko Tadic at checkpoint Orlovci, can you remember whether he was in the military or the police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Police.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can you remember how many other policemen were on duty with him in his shift?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Three to four. It changed, the situation changed from time to time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can you remember the names of any other policemen who were on duty at the same time as Dusko Tadic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Cvijic, Brdar, Tadic. I did not know everybody. I did not know the others.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: How was it that you came to know Dusko Tadic then by name when he was at checkpoint Orlovci?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not know immediately that that was Dusko Tadic. They did not actually -- they did not introduce themselves to me, but some people I used to know from before the war. But then I heard the name and surname of "Tadic" a month, after a month of visits, as we -- and I then later met him in front of his coffee shop and then I realised this was Tadic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: How often did you used to see him at checkpoint Orlovci during that period of June and July?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, very often, quite often.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Were you later aware of the fact that Dusko Tadic was arrested in Germany?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I learned that later, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: How did you learn that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw it and I read it in the media.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you see pictures of Dusko Tadic being arrested?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not -- I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: When you saw Dusko Tadic on duty, did you speak to him at all or familiarise yourself with him? Did you strike up any sort of friendship with him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you strike up any sort of friendship with any of the policemen on duty at checkpoint Orlovci?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was not much socializing. There were just contacts, daily contacts, in the sense that they checked what I was carrying, what I had in my vehicle, and after the initial few days they actually asked me to leave some food for them because they did not receive any regular supplies from the police headquarters. That is how the contact with them began, which lasted for some 40 days during which time I delivered food and for each meal I would leave a certain amount of food for them so that they could eat.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So was your association with Dusko Tadic one that was purely on a working level?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If I can rephrase what I was about to say, did your duties then cease to involve you in delivering food to Kozarac from Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, in early July they ceased.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: What were your duties after that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My Unit was transferred to another location and I was transferred with them, with the rest of the Unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Which location was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My Unit went to Gradacac, Gradacac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can you remember the date that the Unit was transferred to Gradacac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not remember the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did there come a time when your Unit returned from Gradacac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A part of the Operational Unit went to Gradacac while the Rear Supply Units remained in Prijedor. So I actually stayed in Prijedor for a while because I was part of the Rear Supply Units.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you see Dusko Tadic at all after you finished passing through the checkpoint at Orlovci?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: What was the behaviour like of those policemen on duty at Orlovci?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was some official conduct. They actually checked what was -- what the vehicles carried on the Prijedor/Kozarac road and the Prijedor Banja Luka road. This was very courteous, polite but official.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did there come a time when you undertook as part of your duties delivering food to Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can you recollect when that was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot tell you precisely, but I think it was in the autumn, late October, early November. It was raining already and this was, sort of, winter approaching. It was fairly cold at that time and I delivered food to Trnopolje for a month.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: To whom were you delivering food at Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I delivered food for the military policemen who were at that time in Trnopolje.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Whereabouts were those military policemen based?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The military policemen were housed in part of a building which was intended otherwise to be used by the international kitchen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: What do you mean by the "international kitchen"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: People who were in the collection centre of Trnopolje received some supplies from the International Red Cross, and they were served food, food provided by the International Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Was that in a particular building near Trnopolje camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was part of the camp, this was within the camp, within the collection camp of Trnopolje.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: What was the building called at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know. There was nothing written on the building, so I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Whereabouts was the building situated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Just across the school.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Is that the school inside Trnopolje camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: How many times a day did you visit the camp at Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Twice, two times a day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: What times of the day would they be?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the morning, around 10 o'clock in the morning, and again in the afternoon around 6 o'clock, 6 -- 18 hours, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: What sort of supplies would you be taking to Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Cooked food and bread.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: How many people were being supplied with that food?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it was about eight people.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did there come a time when you stopped delivering supplies to that camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Was there any reason for that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: What was the reason?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The camp was disbanded at one point. The Trnopolje camp was disbanded.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can you recollect for how long in terms of time you had been making these deliveries to the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: About a month.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: During this time that you were making deliveries, did you know who was the Camp Commander?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not for sure, but I heard that it was Pero Curguz, I think, that he was the Commander, that he was responsible for the whole camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you ever go into the camp itself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You mean the buildings where people were kept -- no, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you know that it was mainly, almost totally, Muslim people who were held in that camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you ever speak with any of those people who were being held in that camp at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did they speak to you about the conditions that they were being held under?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: In the time that you were there did they say that their conditions were better or worse than they had been previously?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Better.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did they tell you anything about the guards of the camp, whether they were better or worse, when you were delivering?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The conditions were better -- at least that is what they told me - and that is why the military police came there, to make sure that their conditions are better and improved.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Had there been then a change in the guards at the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know what the organisation was for the guards in the camp, neither before nor after the change, but from what I heard from them, I decided that the conditions were incomparably better than they used to be.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You mentioned the military police coming to the camp which was why the conditions were better and improved. Were those military police at the camp at that time that you were delivering?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The military police had one office in that building which I mentioned earlier, and they only supervised the work of the services in the camp and the military policemen were always there when I arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you ever see Dusko Tadic at Trnopolje on those occasions that you were delivering to the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you know if he was the Commander of Trnopolje camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did anyone refer to you or say to you that he was their Commander at the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can you recollect the time when the Trnopolje camp was disbanded, when it ceased to function, as you told us, what date that was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know the date, but I know this was late autumn, just before winter began in 1993 -- 1992, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: That is all I ask. Wait there, please.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Sir, what is your date of birth?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 13th December 1955.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What is your ethnic background?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What is your father's name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Relja.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you were on duty from 22nd May 1992 taking food back and forth to the troops at Kozarac, you would have seen bus loads of Muslim people being taken out of the Kozarac area, would you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You never saw a bus at any stage from 22nd May onwards carrying civilians out of the area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not buses. I saw some leaving a part of Kozarac on foot.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: They were heading towards Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it was in the direction of Trnopolje, I did not come across them in the direction of Prijedor. Some had already been in Prijedor, but mostly in the direction of Trnopolje.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: So when you drove to Kozarac to meet up with the soldiers in order to give them food, you went via Trnopolje, did you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I had to cut across a section of the road which heads to Trnopolje.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You mean you passed the intersection?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: That was the intersection that goes from Kozarac to Trnopolje and the Banja Luka to Prijedor road?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: On the way out of Prijedor you would have passed the Keraterm camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You saw that that changed its function after the war commenced to a camp for holding people that had been cleansed from the Kozarac area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I could not see because there was a truck or something so I could not see anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: A truck or something, what, obstructing your view of the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The facilities, as facilities go, yes, but the exit or the area where people might be, I could not see that from the street.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: But it is a very large building, is it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I could see the building, but where people were kept, I did not see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: But you knew that it was being used as a camp for people who had been cleansed from, in particular, the Kozarac area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I had heard about it. I do not know any details though.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The Orlovci checkpoint that you passed through and where you left food, there was a caravan located on that site, was there not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The guards would go into this caravan from time to time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You had nothing to do with the civilian police, did you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You said in your evidence that you met Tadic later in front of his coffee shop, this is, his coffee shop in Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you say "later", this was later in 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was sometime in June perhaps. I, of course, could not remember the date. 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: In 1992. His coffee shop was operating then, was it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did he appear to be living in the coffee shop or the building near it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it was damaged. The windows of the coffee bar had been damaged in combat operations and he and his brother were trying to do something about it or, rather, to cover it, to put something there so that one could not get in, could not get through.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You stopped and talked to him on this occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I saw that something, was nailing something, so I just stopped and I -- that is when I met this Tadic, that is, I knew his coffee bar, but then -- and I knew him from sight, of course, because we met at the checkpoint. But on that occasion I met him, I learnt that he was Tadic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What was the name of his coffee bar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Can you remember the colour of the building that housed his coffee bar, what outside colour it was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was a private business. I think that the facade -- I think it was brick. I think it had facade -- a part of the building was the residential part, that is where people lived in, and another part had been converted into a coffee bar.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you saw this person who you say was Tadic at the Orlovci checkpoint, that was during the day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You saw him mostly during the day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, quite often.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you see him on every occasion when you delivered food either on the way back or the way forward or what? Can you assist us there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, more or less, because they did not all get off the trailer. One of them would come, check the vehicle and I would give them the food for them and that would be it. Those who were in the caravan, in the trailer, sometimes two of them, would step out or one.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You said that you had through the media become aware of the fact that Tadic had been arrested in Germany. You saw pictures of Tadic when you were watching the media, did you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, at that time I was very busy. I had very many different duties in the army, so I rarely went home and also electricity was very often cut, so it was mostly on the radio.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: But since then you have been able to watch television coverage of these proceedings, have you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When did you first visit the Trnopolje camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Late autumn, late autumn 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: So you had not seen the camp prior to this time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You had not seen the conditions of the camp prior to this time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You had not seen any of the people that were housed in this camp prior to this time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You did not know who ran the camp prior to this time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You knew, however, that the camp existed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you went to the camp, it was made up mostly of old men, women and children?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, they were of all ages.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you say "they were all ages", all ages of women?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Both men and women and children. It was simply the population which had come out of the town wanting to leave the town and, as they themselves affirmed, they were being enabled to leave -- after leaving the town to go to that camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: They wanted to leave the town because they had been cleansed from their homes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I knew some who had been my neighbours and who were not cleansed, who simply because of the living conditions there wanted to leave of their own free will -- at least that is what they were telling me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: So that just all of a sudden in 1992 these people decided that migration was the best option?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is what they said.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Is it not true that most of the military aged men had been removed from the area by this stage?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, there were quite a number of people of my age or even younger in that camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: These were the guards, were they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no, they were of Muslim origin. I am talking about them, who were in the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The guards at the camp when you visited there were from Velika Kladusa, were they, had been recruited from the people that had come in from Velika Kladusa?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you know any of these guards prior to the war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You are not sure, are you, about the precise dates that you were travelling to the camp, this is the Trnopolje camp, sorry?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You know, it was a long time ago and I kept no books of dates or anything and it did not seem important then.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: So if I said to you that rather than being October/November, it could have been mid October through to early December, you would not argue with that, would you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot be more accurate. I know it was autumn. I know it was cold and I knew that the winter was approaching. I know that I covered that route for about a month.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The sanitary conditions in the camp were less than adequate, were they not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My assignment was to bring in food to a facility where the military police were quartered, to deliver this food and go back. I never went into other facilities so that I cannot speak about them in any detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: So you never made any observations whatsoever about the conditions in the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Nothing particular.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You did not see the sanitary conditions in the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You did not see where people were sleeping?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You did not see the food that people were eating?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did see since there was a space, a room next to the police quarters was where the International Red Cross prepared food for them. I think they made tea for them and they distributed bread there. So that is what I know. Other details, I do not know. I know that for the large part they themselves went out to obtain food.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The people in the camp, their clothes were disheveled and dirty, were they not, the prisoners that were being kept in the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To begin with, it was not a camp; it was a reception camp and they were in what they had left their homes in and they were carrying their things and their clothes, and they could change clothes and they could move around. They could go back to their homes and bring over whatever they needed of their belongings, either their things or food.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: So you saw people going home each day, gathering up their possessions and going back and forth to the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You stayed there long enough to observe this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On a couple of occasions there was no transport between Trnopolje/Prijedor, so sometimes I gave them a lift to Prijedor when they asked me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you wear a uniform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What sort of uniform did you wear?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: SMB at first, and then multi-coloured military, I mean camouflage uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were the military guards in the camp supervising the police guards, were they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not know about how military guards were deployed. My only encounter with them was a ramp where I -- when I went -- where I went into Trnopolje, into the camp, that was the only time, the only occasion, the only opportunity, I had to have any contact with any guards whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: There were military guards and police guards there, were there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there were -- military were outside the camp. There was a checkpoint on the road itself and then inside there were police who carried out control.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You did not know who the head of the police was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, there may be some more questions that I would like to ask this witness. I am having some enquiries made now about a matter that I just discovered this morning. I may have the information already, but if your Honours could assist by taking our adjournment now, when I come back I could complete my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: We will stand in recess for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Let us bring the witness in. RAJKO KARANOVIC, recalled Cross-examined by MR. NIEMANN, continued.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann, would you continue, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Witness, I am going to hand you a piece of paper with a number written on it. I am going to ask you whether you could tell me whether that is your telephone number. Perhaps show it to the Defence? (Handed). The telephone number in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is not my telephone number.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Not your number? Have you ever had a telephone number like that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When did you have that telephone number?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What was your address in 1992/93?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My address was in '92 until June Ulica Gavrila Principa, Gavrila Principa Street.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What was it after June?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After June it was Pecanica No. 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: That is entrance C1, is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: That is apartment 65?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: This was an apartment formerly owned by a Muslim family called Campara, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, Campara.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Campara, yes. My pronunciation was not good. The husband's name is Hajrudin?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Hajrudin, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: His wife's name is Adevija -- sorry, I will say that again. His wife's name was Adevija?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not remember the wife's name but I know the husband's name, Hajrudin.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your wife, in fact, worked at the same place as where Hajrudin worked ----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: --- which was the centre for primary education?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You have known Hajrudin for some considerable period of time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You visited this apartment where you lived in Prijedor, is my pronunciation correct when I say Pecanica, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Pecanica settlement, housing development settlement.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Pecanica settlement, yes. You visited that one afternoon about 3 o'clock, 3.00 to 4 o'clock, in July 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not remember the month. I think it might have been July, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: At the time Hajrudin was in the Omarska camp being detained there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, and Hajrudin's wife Adevija was in the apartment with her 10 year old daughter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You had two soldiers with you at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not remember, yes, but I did visit her.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You were armed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You had a knife?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: In fact, you had your knife drawn and not sheafed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You told Adevija and the 10 year old daughter that they were to get out of the apartment by 6 o'clock that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I only gave her a piece of paper. That was a decision which I got, rather, my wife got, to entitle us to the use of this apartment.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You told them that they had to be out at 6 o'clock?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not give any time limit.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You returned to the house at 6 o'clock and the mother, Adevija, and the daughter, 10 year old, were crying and upset?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You told them if they did not get out immediately that they would be killed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: They left immediately, but left all their possessions behind?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They had already removed most of their possessions. I do not know why and on what occasion, but some of their things did remain in the apartment when they left.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You and your family then moved into the apartment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In September, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Some two or three months later, Adevija returned to the apartment and begged you to give her her 10 year old daughter's clothes because she had no clothes for her 10 year old daughter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: She did come, but there were no things left. I did not have anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You told her to get out and that you would not help her?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I said, "These things are not with me any more" and I cannot help her.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The truth is that you would not let her have the clothes for her 10 year old daughter, is it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I had given the clothes to the Red Cross and other things that belonged to that apartment.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Is it not true that when you went to the apartment on the first occasion when you told them to get out, you put a machine gun to the head of the 10 year old daughter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, this is not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You put the machine gun then to the head of the wife, and threatened her with death if she did not get out?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: First of all, we did not have weapons when we entered and, second, I had no reason and no need for that because my wife had the written decision from her school. That was a document which was signed by Hamdija Kahrimanovic, entitling us to the use of the apartment.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The little girl, the little 10 year old daughter, started to cry and you said she was a good actress?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No further questions, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No re-examination, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Witness, I wanted to ask you about the route on which you travelled when you were taking supplies to Kozarac from Prijedor. Perhaps you might look at Exhibit (which is a map) No. 280 which will be passed to you. If you would look at that map you will see Prijedor and Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: And a red road connecting them, do you see that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Was that the road that you travelled on when you were taking food to Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Where do you say this checkpoint was? Was it on that road?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Can you point out where it was on the road?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: I wonder if you would put the map on the overhead? If you would take the pointer which should be lying on the desk in front of you and point out where it is, that is the checkpoint.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It does not say here, but roughly here, round about here. [The witness indicated].

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: No doubt that it was on the red road, the checkpoint?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, here.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: If you keep looking at the map, do you see a yellow road that begins in Prijedor and ends up in Kozarac and a couple of times seems to cross rather like a snake across the red road, do you see that one?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: I think that is -- yes, I think that is called the old road from Prijedor to Banja Luka, is it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: You did not use that road at all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: I see, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VOHRAH
utterances.text: Witness, can you explain how it was possible for an official of the school to transfer the use of the flat from a Muslim family to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VOHRAH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Sir, just a couple of questions. You testified that between June and July some 40 days you passed through this checkpoint where Mr. Tadic was, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Did you see him each day? Is it your testimony that you saw him on 40 different occasions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot be very precise, not 40 occasions, but I saw him frequently manning the checkpoint. It was not Dusko Tadic that came out of the van; some of them remained in the van. One would come out and check what I was carrying and so on, but I saw him frequently.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: What kind of uniform was he wearing when you saw him, if he was wearing a uniform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A police uniform, blue, a blue uniform. That was the old police uniform of the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Was it dark blue or light blue? What kind of blue?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Light blue, I would say.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Is it a solid blue?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, roughly blue, I would say.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: The shirt and the pants were blue?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Do you remember whether Mr. Tadic had a beard when you saw him on these occasions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I think not.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Was he clean shaven?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, maybe he was shaven.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Where was this caravan or trailer that you have spoken of?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To the left of the roadside on the major road between Prijedor and Banja Luka via Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Could you describe the checkpoint? Did it have a barrier that would lift up? Describe it for me.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The checkpoint was organised in a such a way there was this trailer to the left of the road and the road was narrowed artificially and this was broken. So you could not actually go through, drive through, quickly. You had to slow down, go in a zigzag fashion. There was also a sign there, a road sign, which said "Slow down", so that the road was broken, so to speak, and you could not drive through.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: How large was the trailer? Is it the kind of thing that is pulled by a truck?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was a camping caravan.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Is it a part of a truck? Is it like a back on a truck or is it a separate piece?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was separate. It was separate. It was a trailer.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: How long would you estimate the trailer was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Three to four metres, I would say.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Do you know whether this was used by the guards to sleep in if they were not responsible for being outside?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They stayed there. What they did inside, I cannot tell you.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, do you have additional questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, no, thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. I just would like to tender the sheet of paper that the telephone number was written on as a Prosecution Exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Is there any objection, Mr. Kay?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: There is no objection to that, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Do we want to seal it or does it not make any difference?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I do not think it makes any difference.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: OK. What is the number on that?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Exhibit 352 then will be admitted. Is there any objection to this witness being permanently excused?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: There is an objection to him being permanently excused, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Karanovic, you may be recalled by the Tribunal to testify, so you should make yourself available. Keep in touch with Mr. Kay, please, and if you are requested to return then you should return. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Will you do that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you. You are now free to leave. Thank you very much for coming.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Wladimiroff, would you call the next witness, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. The next witness we call is Slavica Lukic. RADOSLAVKA LUKIC, called.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Would you please take the oath that has been handed to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may be seated. Mr. Wladimiroff, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Madam, what is your name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Radoslavka Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: What is your date of birth?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 21st March 1959.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Where were you born?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Dera, Benkovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: What is your nationality or ethnic background?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Where do you live?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Gornji Orlovci, Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Is that a village or a hamlet near Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: How far is that from Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Six kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: What are you doing for a living?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A waitress.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: What is the name of the restaurant where you work?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Now you mean, at this very moment or?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: At this moment, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sana Restaurant.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Where is that restaurant, which place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Are you married?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: What is the name of your husband?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Milovan.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: What is his nationality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Do you know Dusko Tadic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, very well indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Are you related to Dusko Tadic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Are you related to Mira Tadic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Remotely.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Since when do you know Dusko Tadic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Since my childhood, since I have known myself, that is, since early childhood.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Do you know his family?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: His children?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Children, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Madam, are you involved in politics?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Have you ever been involved in politics?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I have no time for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Did you ever discuss politics with Dusko Tadic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Did you ever hear Dusko Tadic talk about politics?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Do you remember him ever expressing nationalistic ideas?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Now let us focus on the time before the conflict broke out. Did you see Dusko Tadic often before the conflict or only occasionally?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From time to time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Where did you live before the conflict broke out?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At Gornji Orlovci.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: That is the same place where you live now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Were you also working as a waitress before the conflict broke out?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: At a certain stage in 1991 relations between the ethnic groups got sour, things escalated and the time got really tense in 1992, did it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Did you continue to work as a waitress in January 1992? Were you working at that time as a waitress?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: What was the name of the restaurant where you worked at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In January, Aero Club, if I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Where was that restaurant?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Across the street from the Balkan Hotel.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Where is the Balkan Hotel?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the very heart of Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Did you ever work at the Hotel Balkan itself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: When did you start to work there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would not remember the exact date, because we were being transferred, depending on the needs or the requirements of the job.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Did you start to work in the Hotel Balkan before the conflict broke out?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I have been there for some 15 or 16 years.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Were you still working as a waitress in April 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Are you able to remember when the Serbs took over control in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it was April 30th, but I am not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: I take it that it was 1992, was it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: When the takeover of Prijedor occurred, did you still work as a waitress at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Did you at any stage before the Serbs took over in Prijedor stop work in Hotel Balkan?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Did you at any stage after the Serbs took over in Prijedor stop work in Hotel Balkan?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, for a short while.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: When was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, after the power had been taken over.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Was that immediately after the takeover or some days later or a week later or weeks later?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it could have been a few days after, three or four days.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: When did you start to work again, when did you return to your work?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was on the waiting list for a while, since I lived at some distance from the town. They used to call those who lived closer to the place. I am not sure I answered this properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: When did you start to work again? When did you return to your work? Was that after a few days, after a week, after a few weeks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, around 20th June or thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: After the takeover of Prijedor, a few days later, you stopped working at the Balkan Hotel in Prijedor and then about 20th June you started to work there again, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: In the meantime you were at home in your village, were you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: What happened in your village in that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I was at home with the children.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Was your husband at home?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Where was your husband then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He had been called up. Later on he was placed under directives of labour but I would not know the dates.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Being mobilized, was he at the front?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was a driver. He drove a truck.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: When you returned to your work, about 20th June 1992, did you continue to work at the Balkan Hotel restaurant?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: What were your working hours?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I worked from 7.00 to 3.00 for a while every day for some time, and subsequently there would be such shifts one whole day, one day off, and that is how we worked depending then on the needs.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Did you work in other shifts too? You have just indicated that you worked from 7.00 until 3 o'clock in the afternoon, did you also do your job in the evenings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did. I worked. For a while I worked from 7.00 until 3.00 and then I worked the whole day or, rather, from 7 o'clock in the morning until the evening hours, that is, 8.00 or 9.00. It varied depending on the curfew which means that I did work evenings too.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: What was the implication of the curfew? You were not able to travel or what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After the curfew one could not move around.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Since you were living in Orlovci, you would not move from the restaurant towards your house or from your house to the restaurant, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I went -- I took bicycle or I hiked, hitchhiked. I tried to manage somehow.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Do you remember the times of the curfew? When did it start and when did it stop?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It started, I believe, at 9.00 until 6 o'clock in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: After the takeover in Prijedor, troubles started at Kozarac, did they not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Do you remember when Kozarac was attacked?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The exact date, I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Do you remember the month?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: May, I think it was May.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Was that on a day during the week or in the weekend?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: That is all right. Was that attack in the evening or in the day time, can you remember that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Day time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Where were you at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At home with my family.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Was your husband also at home?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Was he at the front?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, here on the line with everybody else.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Was that in Slovenia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was at Orlovci.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Did you continue to work without interruption after June 20th 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: That was at the Hotel Balkan in Prijedor, was it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was a coffee bar, a coffee bar.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: That coffee bar was in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I started working there right afterwards, even though there were transfers back to the hotel.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Living in Gornji Orlovci and working in Prijedor means that you travelled to Prijedor to do your job and from Prijedor back home, did you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Am I right in thinking that you just a few moments ago gave evidence that you travelled by bike or sometimes a vehicle would take you to Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Excuse me, your Honour. I do not think that counsel is right in his assumption that that was the previous evidence and at this point I would object to leading questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: I have no problem in rephrasing that, your Honour. As a matter of fact ----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not understand this.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: As a matter of fact, my learned friend just tells me from the transcript it appears that that was the evidence indeed. (To the witness): But, nevertheless, by what means of transportation did you travel to Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I took a bicycle if the weather was nice, and when the weather was bad, then I tried to manage somehow, that is, we would hitchhike some vehicle and got transportation. There was also a checkpoint and vehicles were being stopped there and we asked the policemen to stop a car for us and give us a lift to the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: You referred to a checkpoint, is that at Orlovci?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the checkpoint was at Orlovci.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Is that a checkpoint on the road to Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Is that road the main road from Prijedor leading via Kozarac to Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the main road.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Is that checkpoint near your house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is, very near.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Can you tell the Court how near in metres, the distance?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: About 150, 200 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Could you see the checkpoint from your house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Can I have Prosecution Exhibit 280 shown to the witness, please? (Handed). Madam, please take your time and familiarise yourself with that map. First, I would ask you to look at the map where you live, if that is on the map.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have found the place where I live.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Then look to the map again and try to locate where the checkpoint is. Are you able to find it? Take your time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it is here.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, would you be so kind as to put the map on the overhead projector, please? If I may ask the technical booth to focus a little bit more on the map? Mr. Usher, could you give the witness the pointer, please? Madam, I am going to ask you to use that pointer, not on your screen but on the map on your right-hand side, on the map which is on your right-hand side, please -- the usher will help you -- look to the map which is on your right-hand side. Now look at the map again ----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: --- and please point where you live on the map?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [The witness indicated] Here.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Are you able to point where the checkpoint is on the main road? Do you see the main road?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the main road.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Do you see a red line on that map, a horizontal red line?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please speak into a microphone?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Witness, could you look at the whole map? Do you see a red road on that map running from Prijedor to Kozarac? That is a yellow road, is it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: But if you go down with the pointer there is a red road, do you see that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Yes. Am I right in thinking that that red line is the main road between Prijedor and Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Well, thank you. You have been very helpful. Let us forget about the map and continue with the examination. You told us, madam, that the checkpoint was about 200, perhaps 250 metres away from your house at Gornji Orlovci, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: She said it was 150 to 200.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Can you describe that checkpoint? What did it look like?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know what it looked like. I do not really know how to answer this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Right. Let me break the question down in into smaller questions. Was there a barrier over the road or was there not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there were barriers. Yes, there were barriers.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Was the road open for traffic or were there obstacles on the road?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were some obstacles on the road so that the vehicles could be halted easier.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Was there a facility for those who were on duty to stay, for example, when it was bad weather, was there a house or portacabin or a caravan or what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there was a trailer, a camp trailer, a camp caravan, something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Was that a large one or a small one? Could you describe that caravan, please, or that trailer, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Why, an ordinary trailer, people who worked went into rest.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Could you describe the measurement of that trailer in metres? How long it was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In metres, well, three metres or thereabouts, as far as I can recall and if I am able to judge.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Were there trees at that point?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Am I right in thinking that one of the trees was a very large one?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there was a walnut tree, very tall.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Did you see Dusko Tadic on duty at this checkpoint?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: How long after the attack on Kozarac -- no, let me rephrase that. You started to work again, as you told us, about 20th June 1992 in Prijedor, did you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: I take it that going to your work you passed that checkpoint?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Did you see Dusko Tadic at that checkpoint?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Did you see him right away on the first day you went again back to your work or was that later?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not remember very well. Maybe on the first day, but certainly I did see him there as I travelled to work and back.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Did you see him there regularly or just occasionally?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I saw him when I went if he was on duty. If he was not on duty on that shift I could not see him of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: When you were on your way to your work, as you told us about your working hours, did you see him more than once a week or twice a week or more times a week at that checkpoint?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would say several times a week.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Do you remember how many people were working at that checkpoint?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Five to six people as far as I could notice, as far as I remember, but I never paid much attention to the number of people which was not of interest for me. I think it was five to six people who were manning the checkpoint.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Did you know these men, except for Dusko Tadic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I knew some people.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Those five to six men you saw, were they working together? Did they have the same shifts?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know how they arranged their work. I just passed through and passing through I used to see them, but how exactly they arranged their shifts and so on I just do not know. How this was all regulated is unclear to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: When you saw Dusko Tadic at point Orlovci, would that be on your way to Prijedor or did you also see him on other occasions while you were at home at Orlovci?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He used to, he would come to my house to have coffee. They were helping me, doing me a favour when I was travelling so I thought I would give something in return.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Could they not make their own coffee in that trailer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Probably, they probably could, but he would come, he would come to my house, also to my neighbour's house. This was my next door neighbour, a woman.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Just to chat and to drink a cup of coffee?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, to have a chat, to have some conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Does that mean that Dusko Tadic would then walk up the lane to your house on these occasions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he came on foot. He came on foot. This was very close. There was no use driving.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Did he come by himself or was he sometimes with other men?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I remember that once or on several occasions one of his colleagues was with him, those who were also manning the checkpoint with him at the same time, but I do not know who that was, I do not remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Do you remember how long Dusko Tadic had been working there at point Orlovci, at that checkpoint?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: You told us that you started to work again about June 20th 1992. Did you see him ----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: --- throughout the month of June?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Did you see him the next month in July 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In July?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: In July.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Did you see him as regular as you did before, during the month of June?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know that I would see him as I went to my work. I think this was regular, yes, regular.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: There were no changes in July, I mean you saw him less or more? It was the same, or was it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it was the same, the same as before. This again depended on their shifts, and so Dusko was on this checkpoint.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Did that become a kind of routine seeing him there, is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am sorry, I am going to object to leading questions. They are becoming more frequent.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I will sustain the objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: I will withdraw that question, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: You can rephrase it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: [To the witness]: Seeing Dusko Tadic at that checkpoint and having him on occasions drinking coffee with you, what was the behaviour of Dusko? Was there anything peculiar or was it all normal?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was all normal, normal behaviour and he would just take a walk, come and visit.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Besides seeing Dusko Tadic at point Orlovci, did you see him elsewhere in that period of time or later in that year?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw him in the restaurant, in the hotel restaurant.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: That would be Hotel Balkan?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Balkan Hotel, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: That is in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Are you able to tell us on how many occasions you saw him there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot tell you how many times, but on several occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Did you see him alone or with someone else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw him with his wife.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Was that during the period of June/July you saw him, also saw him at point Orlovci or was that later on in 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot remember now. I do not remember at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Did you know where Dusko Tadic lived when he was on duty at point Orlovci?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not. I think he lived -- he lived in Prijedor I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Do you have any idea which quarter of Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I do not know. He never told me and I was not interested.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Do you know what happened to his house in Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Did you ever see him at the police station of Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I never went there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: That is all I ask, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: We will stand in recess until 2.30. 1.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: RADOSLAVKA LUKIC, recalled.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Wladimiroff?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: We had concluded the examination, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Very good. Thank you. Cross-examination, Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
