utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mrs. Lukic, you indicated that you were a relative of Mira Tadic. What is the nature of that relationship?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, distant. We were distant relatives. My mother and Mira's mother are cousins, again distantly removed. I mean removed, several times removed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You grew up in the area of Dera?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Where was Mira from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The hamlet of Vidovici.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You knew her from the time of childhood as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: How did you happen to know Dusko Tadic from childhood? Was that because you were living in Dera?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: While going to the school in Kozarac and that is also where I met Dusko because I went to primary school in Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: When did you move away from the area of Dera?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I married.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That was approximately how long before the conflict in 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What do you mean? I did not understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: In what year did you marry?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I need concentration -- '79.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You indicated during your earlier testimony that you were trying to or you were happy to repay favours by serving coffee and welcoming Dusko Tadic at your home when he visited?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, yes, I was happy to make him a cup of coffee and do him a favour since he did me favours, things like that. You know, those favours -- I have already mentioned them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I take it that during the occasions he visited sometimes those visits were for shorter periods, sometimes they were for longer periods?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He came to see me not more than two or three times there in front of the house. He would not even come into the house. It was in front of the house.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You would bring him coffee and talk?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would bring the coffee and he would say that he was leaving again on his business, but that was a favour I did because it is a custom to have a cup of coffee.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You mentioned that he brought a colleague with him once when he came to visit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: OK. Was that someone you had seen at the checkpoint before that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he was with them at the checkpoint. He was with him at the checkpoint.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Had you seen that particular person with Mr. Tadic at the checkpoint a few times or many times?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A couple of times, well, often but I do not know whether they were always on the same shift. They were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You mentioned that among the people who were on the shift with Mr. Tadic you knew some of them. Who did you know?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Objection, your Honour. That was not the evidence, as far as I remember that.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I would be happy -----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: You see, I do not remember so I would suggest that you rephrase the question and that will solve it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You were asked earlier during the examination about the five or six men you saw on the shift with Mr. Tadic, and asked if you knew some of them other than Mr. Tadic. Do you recall saying that you did know some of them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I knew -- I do not know his name, people call him Brada, but I do not know what his proper name is. I simply was not interested to learn.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Was Brada a proper name or a nickname?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was a nickname.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Do you know what that nickname means?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I guess he had a beard. He had a beard.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Was he the person who visited your house with Mr. Tadic on the occasion Mr. Tadic brought a colleague?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did you know any other people at the checkpoint who were with Mr. Tadic on any occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I cannot recall any people really because they changed, and I did not pay much attention to who those people were or what their names were. It was simply passing by. I mean, I really know Tadic best than any other of them -- better than any other of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sometimes because of the distance you had to travel and the weather conditions, it was helpful for you to find a ride into Prijedor, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Was that one of the favours that Mr. Tadic or the others at the checkpoint helped you with?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: On occasion was one or another of them good enough to give you a ride into Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, usually they would stop a car and then ask those people to take us.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: On occasion when there was not a car that was in a position to do so, would they be willing to take you into town themselves?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no, and then I was late for work!

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your husband was mobilized during this time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Where was he stationed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot really recall that, those early days. I think -- I cannot remember where he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: On occasion did Mr. Tadic or any of those at the checkpoint help you out with some duties at your home, moving furniture or doing some things that you could not do without your husband present?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Things -- I did not understand that. Could you repeat it, please? What things do you have in mind? Tadic came only two or three times to my home and then I saw him at my neighbour's from whom he bought cheese or milk from time to time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: What is that neighbour's name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Gordana, Vlacina. Gordana Vlacina.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: How far from your home did she live?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Very near, I think third, third house, I should say.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You mentioned during your testimony earlier that you did not recall hearing Mr. Tadic express Serbian nationalist sentiments to you. Do you recall hearing any Serb during that time express Serbian nationalist sentiments?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Do you recall hearing them over the radio or reading them in the newspaper?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not have much time to read newspapers or ----

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mrs. Lukic, you mentioned Gordana Vlacina. Was she also a friend of Dusko Tadic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not think so. I do not think they were friends. We simply met there, since Dusko was nearby at the checkpoint and that is when we -- when she -- I think that is when she met him at that time. I do not know whether they knew each other before.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did the three of you ever get together during that period of time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: How long did you continue to see Dusko Tadic at the Orlovci checkpoint?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot really exactly how long. It was that summer, I think, but how long, I do not remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Was your husband a friend of Dusko Tadic as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, nothing special. They knew each other because our house was there and Dusko was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Are you still in contact with Mira Tadic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sometimes I happen across her in the town. We both work, work, but we do not really make appointments and meet.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: When did you last see her?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw her, well, when I was working, as when I go to work then I meet Mira who also goes to work, but we did not even meet, stop and talk. I mean, I really mean we never discussed this or anything like it. All I asked her was: "Shall we go? If we are invited, shall we go?" She said: "Yes, well, if you want to, do", and that was all, very briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: When did that conversation take place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It could have been some 15 days ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Where was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the street. We just met in the street. We just happened to meet in the street.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: When had you last seen her before that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Before that, well, I did not see her. I do not -- I do not remember that I saw her.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: What about Mr. Tadic's brother Mladen, are you friends with him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Have you happened to see him in Prijedor or Kozarac since the time of the conflict?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: What about Mr. Tadic's brother Ljubo, do you know him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I knew him since my childhood, but now I hardly know him at all any longer. Since he lives in Banja Luka, I simply do not see him.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Have you spoken with him since the time of the conflict?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That is all. Thank you, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Wladimiroff?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Nothing arises, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Is there any objection to Mrs. Lukic being permanently excused?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour, there is.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mrs. Lukic, you are free to leave now, but you may be recalled as a witness, so you should make yourself available. You may go home, of course, keep in touch with Mr. Wladimiroff and if he tells you that you need to return, then you will return. Will you do that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I will.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Fine. Thank you very much. You are not permanently excused. You are excused now. Thank you very much for coming.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, would you call your next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Nada Vlacina, please.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: We thought we would meet with counsel in closed session for a few minutes before we adjourn this evening, so maybe at 5.15 or so?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. NADA VLACINA, called.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Would you please take the oath that is being handed to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I shall speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you. You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Is your name Nada Vlacina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Do you live in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do, I live in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: For how long have you lived in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Since 1974 until the present day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Do you know Dusko Tadic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: How long have you known him for?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have known him since the summer of 1983.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: How did you come to know Dusko Tadic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Dusko and my husband worked together at Banja Luka at the Cajavec Company and that year, right, in 1983 Dusko and his wife Mira came to visit us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: What work was done at the factory where Dusko Tadic worked with your husband?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you ever visit Dusko Tadic at his family home?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Kozarac, only following the death of his father, but before I used to come, they lived in a private home not far from their present house, so we would come and visit frequently.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Were you friendly with other members of the Tadic family?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, we did not visit very frequently but, yes, I knew the whole family.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you know that Dusko Tadic had a cafe in Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I knew that, and I was in that cafe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: How often did you visit that cafe?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the cafe was opened only after the death of his father, and I was there two to three times, but we came and visited each other as families. So when we visited him, he took us into the cafe to show us around, to have a drink and so on, but we did not stay long. We were not ordinary cafe visitors.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: At the time of the conflict in Kozarac in 1992, were you living in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Which part of Prijedor was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was the Pecani settlement. This is a housing complex. There were no other public buildings. There was no hospital. There was simply a school plus family accommodations and shops. This is a district, a residential district somewhat removed from the city, from the centre of the city, some 15 minutes away. This is a new development built in the 80s, during the 80s, 1985 or thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Are there a number of apartment blocks where families live in that particular district of Pecani?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All of the buildings, in fact, were housing buildings plus shops, of course, and a school. There was no medical facility. There was no other public building there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you know Dusko Tadic's wife Mira?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I know her. I know Mira. I know the children. I know his mother, his brothers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: For how long have you known Mira Tadic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mira and Dusko came to visit us together. They had been swimming and in the evening after the swim and the excursion they came to visit us. So I know her since 1983, for the summer of 1983, I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So the occasion that you met Dusko Tadic for the first time was also the occasion that you met Mira Tadic, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, on the same time -- the same day at the same time because they came to our house together in the evening, just early evening before dusk.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Were you aware of the conflict starting in Kozarac in May 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I heard about that. We bought our apartment and we moved there because we had not lived there before. We used to live -- me and my husband used to live in the centre of the city. Then my husband was given an apartment and I was arranging it, furnishing it, and when the shooting started I actually realised that we were at war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Do you happen to remember what the date of that was, when you heard that shooting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The first shooting started on 22nd May 1992. This was a Friday. There was something not far from Hambarine, but I cannot tell you about these events. I can only tell you what I heard from other people, from what I heard from the media. I did not see anything with my own eyes. I did not -- I was not involved in these events. But the first clashes, as far as I remember, were on 22nd May in the early hours of the evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: On 22nd May were you in Prijedor at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I was at home in my apartment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: In the days after 22nd May when the conflict continued, did you remain living in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I did. All the time I was there, all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you at around that time of May and the months or the month after May move out of Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, we did not. I did not have anywhere to go.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you see Dusko Tadic in Prijedor after the conflict had started in Kozarac or Hambarine, as you have described it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you remain living in Pecani during this period?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, all that time, throughout that time I lived there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you ever see Dusko and Mira Tadic in that area of Pecani where you were living?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw -- met them for the first time, I think it was, the second half of July. Then I saw them for the first time. But I saw Dusko the last time, I moved into my apartment on 26th April, that was Sunday, and that was when we brought our furniture into the house. This was the Orthodox Easter. I had my first lunch in my new apartment. I remember that day very well. On Monday was 27th of April. Then on Tuesday or Wednesday in April I saw him, and after that I never saw him again. I met him in town. We just stopped there and I said: "What are you doing? Where are you going?" and he says: "Well, I am going to fetch Mira at Sanski Most". Then Mira's sister came along and I said: "Hello", "Goodbye" and so, "See you later. We are moving to a new apartment. We are too busy". I tried to explain where the apartment was and that was it. That, as far as I remember, that happened on 27th or 28th April.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: When you saw Dusko Tadic on this occasion in April 1992, you had just moved into your own new apartment, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, a day or two, I am not quite certain, but two to three days.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You said that you had bought that apartment, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, we did not buy that apartment. That apartment was given to my husband by his Company.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Right, and which Company was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Ljubija iron mines. That is where my husband worked at that time. His first job was a Cajavec in Banja Luka. I do not know what he was doing there, but this was a short period of time. He did not stay there for a long time, but they worked together, with Dusko, and they travelled together and they were away practically all day and they went to work, came back from work. Then Dusko left that Company, then my husband left that Company, came to Montmontaze and then from Montmontaze to the Ljubija mines.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The apartment you described in Pecani, that is where you are living at the moment, is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we still live there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Was that the apartment you got on April 26th 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right, right, that was the first apartment that we got. Before that I lived with my family in my father's apartment, and together with my brother, his wife, daughter, there were seven of us in 51 square metres apartment. That was a small apartment, and my parents were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Was that in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that was in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: When you got your apartment in Pecani, did the Tadic family ever live near you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Tadic family moved. I do not know the exact date. I tried to refresh my memory, to decide when that happened, but in late afternoon I went shopping. I visited my brother and his wife and then I saw the two of them, Tadic and his wife, namely, and they told me: "Well, we have got a flat at Pecani". They did not know which building that was because the buildings were very poorly marked, B1, C1. They knew only the block. They only knew the entrance, but they could not find it. I know that my children remained. This was a nice day and I remember that day which was nice and peaceful, and then they actually went into the apartment which they had been allocated.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you ever visit them in that apartment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Two or three days, four days later, I do not know exactly when. I did not visit them at once. They said they would come to me for coffee and have coffee with me. They did not come. The following day they had to do some work in the apartment. There were some things there. So then they went to Banja Luka to bring their children, their grandmother and so on. So I cannot tell you whether it was three, five, six days and then I visit them for the first time. We started visiting each other more regularly because in that part of Prijedor they knew nobody. They had no friends or relatives. They had no acquaintances, but there were no real friends of theirs there. We also had no friends, really, just a few acquaintances but no real friends. We were new people on the block, so to speak.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So at that time that you saw Dusko Tadic and his wife Mira, the rest of the family were in Banja Luka, they told you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they were there. I only met the two of them who came to inspect the apartment while -- and then I do not know who went, Dusko or Mira or together, they went to bring the rest of the family, and only when everybody was there actually I came to visit for the first time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Do you know if Dusko Tadic was working at that time that you saw him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Do you know where that was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He worked at Orlovci. There was a police checkpoint and that is where he worked. I only learned about that later when we started talking to each other, tell each other about what we are doing, how we are living, and so on. So he explained to me where he worked, and I had my mother-in-law there. We had no electricity at that time. Often there was no water supply. Once or twice a week I went to the village and I brought some -- we got food there and that helped.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: What was the name of the village where your mother-in-law was living?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Gornji Orlovci.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: What is the name of your mother-in-law? What is her first name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Draginja Vlacina, while the father-in-law died before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: When you visited your mother-in-law, did you ever see Dusko Tadic at Orlovci checkpoint?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Because there was no public transportation at that time, the village of Orlovci was about four, four and a half kilometres, and we had to go on foot for an hour and a half with my children, and an hour and a half return journey. So we went on foot for three hours in a single day. Because we were in contact on a daily basis, I knew when he would be manning the checkpoint, so then I would not -- I would not have to return on foot because he would be stopping a passing car and they would take us to Prijedor; and if it was the end of their shift, they would also take us into the police car. Since we were three of us, we could not all fit into the police car so he would stop another passing car to take us. Whenever I went, I actually made it a point, my children are 14 and 13 now, they were little children, and it was difficult for them to walk and we -- I had nothing in my apartment, I had no gas, no oven, so we would go into the village. We would be eating breakfast or dinner and lunch, lunch and dinner, and the mother-in-law would be cooking something.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So how often did you see him at this checkpoint at Orlovci?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot tell you precisely, but often.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can you remember when this was, when he was working at the checkpoint?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He worked there in that period, when he arrived in Prijedor. When we met, he told me. I did not know where he worked. Maybe he had been working at Orlovci even before, before meeting us, but I never went there. My mother-in-law lives about a kilometre, a kilometre and a half, off the main road. There was an old road, and I usually took the old road because that was a short cut. It was closer to my house, to my mother-in-law's house. So it was better for me to use the old road. I did not even know that I could go to the checkpoint and that the police would help me find a car to bring me back to Prijedor, but he told me then. He said: "I am working there. I can help you". So I then actually then returned on that -- through that checkpoint. It is possible that he had worked there before.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you know anyone else that he was working with at that checkpoint at Orlovci?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was another man called Brada, I do not know the name, and Brdar, Brdar. I remember on one occasion I actually came back with them, myself, the children, Dule and Brdar whose first name I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you know Brdar at the time, that that was his name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think I did or I may have heard the name because they would call each other. One of them they called "Brada" because he had a beard and again that is how I learned the name. For Brada, I do not know his real name. Brdar, I remember him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The one called Brada, that was a nickname, was it, because he had a thick beard?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that was a nickname.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: This period that you are talking about, the period when you saw Dusko Tadic in Prijedor and you saw him at the checkpoint Orlovci, was that before or after the conflict in Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After the conflict in Kozarac. This was in the second half of June.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: When you saw Dusko Tadic on these occasions at the checkpoint Orlovci, what was his behaviour like?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know -- normal. They were checking traffic. Each car that came along had to stop. They would check the documents. I do not know what they were looking for, but then after a while the car would be let pass -- let to pass and go.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Nothing further, thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Cross-examination Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Just one moment, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mrs. Vlacina, other than you and your husband and your immediate family, did you have other family members living in opstina Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did you have brothers and sisters?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have one brother.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And his name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Milan.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: What was your husband's position with the Ljubija mine company?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was a graduate mechanical engineer. What exactly he was doing, I do not know, but he was in charge. He was a manager of something, but I do not know what.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: As a manager of the mine, he was entitled to an apartment which was provided by the mining company?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, let me explain this. This apartment was an apartment for the personnel department, so to speak, in the sense that they could give it to somebody important. My husband was the most senior engineer and he was the last one who had not got an apartment and was, therefore, given the apartment by the Ljubija mines.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That apartment was, as you indicated, in the Pecani settlement which was a new development in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right, Pecani B1, and in that apartment before us there lived a family, a Muslim family. This was a colleague of my husband, a Muslim. His wife came from a mixed marriage. In 1991, in December 1991, they moved to Australia, the whole family left for Australia and, if necessary, I can give you the name of that person. So, the answer was -- the flat was then kept by his father for a while. Then they realised that they had found a good job in Australia, and so he actually had emigrated to Australia and did not intend to return. Then the father actually returned the flat to the mines, to the mine company, and my husband being the next on the list of those who were supposed to give the flat got it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The Pecani area is an area of high rise apartment buildings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I think that B2 -- in B2 there are several buildings there and this is one of the blocks, and I think that one such unit has eight floors, and I think there was another. Only one part of the building has eight floors because there are several entrances. In one building there are four entrances, in another one there are five. I do not know. My building specifically has six floors, the building in which I live.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Is that the most modern, most recent, development in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is, yes, and B1, that building where I live now, it was built two or three years -- no, I do not know when it was finished, when it was completed, but they are the most modern buildings in Prijedor and these are nice apartment blocks, all of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: When you visited the Tadic family in their new apartment in Pecani, did you notice whether or not the flat was empty or whether it was fully furnished?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, very little furniture was left in the flat. It was all unusable and the basic things were lacking such as, for instance, television set or, for instance, a wooden stove. There were very few things left. I know there was a table in a very poor condition, all cracked, kept together with scotch tape, a settee or something, but it was all very old in that room in which I was, that living room.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did you know who the previous owner or occupant of the apartment had been?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no, I did not know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You were not told that the previous occupant had been Hasan Tulundzic, the head of the SUP?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I heard that. I heard that. But I did not live there. I did not know anyone there, except here and there. I mean, I did not live there before that because by the time I got settled in my house, in my apartment, everything was over. I had no time to meet anyone or to learn where everybody lived. I had a friend who was a Muslim, and when electricity and water supply were cut off she came to me because I had a water pump, and then she explained where she lived and explained that she had a stove with wood. So I spent for a while cooking at her place, and I had another friend, a Croat, who was married to a Serb, and they were the only two persons until the Tadic's arrived and then again they were the only people whom I knew in Pecani.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: But you knew that Hasan Tulundzic and other Muslims of the area had been forced to leave because they were Muslim?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know these things. Listen, people went in different ways. Some went this way, some that way, but how individuals left, I do not know. I would not be able to answer that question because some people left of their own free will. For instance, my husband's colleague, that is the one into whose flat we moved, the man himself before the war, before anything happened, simply left Prijedor. He had asked for an emigration visa, obtained it all from Australia because he was a specialist, an engineer, got a nice job there, took his family. People left, everybody who could have left Prijedor, all those who could find a job elsewhere and settle elsewhere, that is what I do know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did you know that many of those who left Prijedor town, for example, ended up in Omarska or Keraterm before they left opstina Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know. Of my friends, Muslims, Croats, with whom I and my husband socialised, I think 80 or 90 per cent of them were that large number. Almost all our friends were either Muslims or Croats, even acquaintances. They are all alive and well. Except for one, none of them were in Omarska and I heard about Omarska only later. That friend of mine, that Muslim, in whose house I used to cook, her husband was also a mechanical engineer. He had been to university with my husband and the two of us, I mean, she and I were together at school, and he was in Prijedor and he left but he had not been to any of those places. I am telling you about my friends, about my acquaintances, about people with whom we socialised, with whom we had contact, I and my husband.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You are not suggesting that 80 to 90 per cent of the Muslims who lived in opstina Prijedor before the conflict remain there today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I do not know how many of them are there now. I simply do not know the figures. I do not know how many Muslims there are. I know there are, but I did not how many of them were there before the war or how many there are now. We still have a Muslim family, purely Muslim family, a man who was with my husband in the same company and with whom we still have good relations, and that is a purely Muslim family.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So you are not sure if there was any decline in the Muslim population of opstina Prijedor since the war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Are you suggesting that those people left of their own free will?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would not know that. I mean, I simply do not know. Some went of their own volition, some -- my life was very hard in 92. It was a struggle for survival, what to give children for breakfast, what for lunch, what for dinner. All I could think about came down to that, how to feed my family.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did your husband continue to work for the mining company during the spring and summer of 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no, he did not work there. He was under directives of labour since '93, since April '93.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Where was he working and what was he doing in the spring and summer of 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the mine. In summer of '92 he did not work. My husband -- the last day he worked was Friday 22nd May, it was Friday, until April 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Before that which complex of the mining company had he worked in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Omarska mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That is all I have. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Just one matter: I would like you to look at this photograph, madam, and tell me if you recognise it. I tender it before the Court as D67. Do you recognise that photograph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do. This is the building, B2, and above it, I think this is where Dusko Tadic's flat was. This is the passage here, this third window here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Perhaps that photograph there (which is the only one I have) could be shown to Mr. Tieger at this stage and then put on the overhead projector?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Is there any objection to -- are you offering Defence 67?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, I am, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Any objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, your Honour, no objection.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: 67 will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. If we could put it on our monitor? Madam, if you look to the right of you, you will see the photograph on the table to your right. Could you indicate with the pointer which was the flat of Mr. Tadic -- not on the television screen but actually on the photograph itself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [The witness indicated on the photograph] This one here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Was that long enough on the monitor for the Court to see? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: That is all I ask, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mrs. Vlacina, was your husband a member of the SDS Party?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no, no, never. No member of my family, not one of my friends, was ever a member of either SDS or SDA, neither Muslims nor Serbs, and that perhaps was very unfortunate for me because when the war came, I mean, none of us had anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Nothing arises, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Is there any objection to Mrs. Vlacina being permanently excused?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: There is, your Honour, and, if I may, if I could ask one final question? Sorry, I realise that ----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Yes, fine. I also have a question I think now. You go first.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Ma'am, you may have answered this question earlier, but what is your husband first name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Must I answer that question? Milan Vlacina, mechanical engineer.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mrs. Vlacina -- help me pronounce your name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Nada Vlacina.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: You said right at the end of your testimony that, unfortunately, you were not a member of the SDS and no one in your family, you say, was a member of the SDS, and because you were not when the war came you had nothing. What do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, until the very last day I did not believe that a war would break out, that there would be a war, because we could not hear anything from anyone, neither from Muslims nor from Serbs. I mean, those people with whom I had in contact, that we had contact with, nobody knew anything, because none of them were close to the authorities or participating authorities. Nobody went to any meetings or anything. We were simply all waiting and hoping that there would not be any war. When I moved into that flat, I had most of the things, I had most of the things, but I lacked curtains or carpets, or things, and I had bought all these things. So, what money I had I invested into the flat. Had I known what would happen, I would have, you know, kept that money and, therefore, tried to feed the family with it. In my circle, among my friends, neither Muslims nor Serbs, nobody knew anything. We saw that something was in the offing, but nobody knew anything specific and I had very many friends among Muslims, very nice people, great workers, not intellectuals only, there were craftsmen and engineers, and it hit us all in the same way, all of us, and that Muslim family helped me more during that war than I would have been able to help them under the circumstances.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Nothing arises, thank you, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Are you asking that this witness be available just in case you want to have her recalled, is that what you are saying?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That is correct, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: OK. Ma'am, you are excused today and you are free, of course, to go home but you should be available because you may possibly be recalled as a witness. So you should keep in touch with Mr. Kay. He will advise you if you are to return to the Tribunal to testify again. Will you do that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, all right.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much for coming. (The witness withdrew).

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, your next witness?

utterances.speaker: MISS DE BERTODANO
utterances.text: Your Honour, the next witness is Sava Vokic. Your Honour, if I might say, this witness would prefer to have the oath read to her so she can repeat it. SAVA VOKIC, called

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Ma'am, this is the oath that I am now reading; would you repeat after me, "I" and your name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Vokic Sava. (The witness was sworn, having duly repeated the words of the oath as read by the learned Presiding Judge).

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Fine. Thank you. You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: MISS DE BERTODANO
utterances.text: Witness, is your name Sava Vokic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MISS DE BERTODANO
utterances.text: What is your date of birth?

utterances.speaker: MISS DE BERTODANO
utterances.text: Where do you live?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Velko Palanciste, Prijedor. Velko Palanciste.

utterances.speaker: MISS DE BERTODANO
utterances.text: How far is Velko Palanciste from Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: About three kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MISS DE BERTODANO
utterances.text: How far is it from Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From Kozarac, about 20, 22 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MISS DE BERTODANO
utterances.text: Are you married?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS DE BERTODANO
utterances.text: What is your husband's name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Slavko Vokic.

utterances.speaker: MISS DE BERTODANO
utterances.text: How long have you lived in Velko Palanciste?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I have lived there for -- it will be about 20 years.

utterances.speaker: MISS DE BERTODANO
utterances.text: Do you know Dusko Tadic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know Dusko Tadic since he was born, when he was born.

utterances.speaker: MISS DE BERTODANO
utterances.text: Is he a relation of yours?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not, not really -- yes, a little bit. My husband's relative, but my husband is no longer with us, and so .....

utterances.speaker: MISS DE BERTODANO
utterances.text: How is Dusko Tadic related to your husband?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I think that they were distant cousins with his mother, distant. They were cousins.

utterances.speaker: MISS DE BERTODANO
utterances.text: Do you know the parents of Dusko Tadic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I do know his parents.

utterances.speaker: MISS DE BERTODANO
utterances.text: What are their names?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: His parents?

utterances.speaker: MISS DE BERTODANO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Ostoja and Staka Tadic.

utterances.speaker: MISS DE BERTODANO
utterances.text: Now you have told us that you knew Dusko Tadic since he was born?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS DE BERTODANO
utterances.text: How often would you see Dusko Tadic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When he was younger or smaller, of course, it was more often. As the time went by, of course, less and less, and so .....

utterances.speaker: MISS DE BERTODANO
utterances.text: Do you remember the conflict which broke out in Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not quite. It started but I do not really remember it well. Yes, there was fire. I was far away and, of course, everybody has his own duties, things to do.

utterances.speaker: MISS DE BERTODANO
utterances.text: Can you remember approximately what time, when the conflict in Kozarac happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To tell you frankly, to tell you the truth, I remember Jovica Zgonjanin was killed. Then we heard he was killed and then a clash began and went on. That is what I remember.

utterances.speaker: MISS DE BERTODANO
utterances.text: Do you remember what year this was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Why, I think it was in '92.

utterances.speaker: MISS DE BERTODANO
utterances.text: Do you remember the month of that year?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It must have been around late May. I would -- do not ask me the date, but I think it was late May.

utterances.speaker: MISS DE BERTODANO
utterances.text: Thank you. In the couple of years before the conflict, had you seen Dusko Tadic often?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MISS DE BERTODANO
utterances.text: How often would you have seen him during that time, approximately?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To tell you the truth, I did see him on 2nd May. That was when I saw him. It was 2nd May. That was that date.

utterances.speaker: MISS DE BERTODANO
utterances.text: How do you remember that date?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I remember that date because my mother-in-law -- how shall I tell you? We were burying -- no, it was the first, it was the anniversary of her death and he was in Banja Luka, and then I remembered because relatives came from Banja Luka. That is when I saw him.

utterances.speaker: MISS DE BERTODANO
utterances.text: What relation was she to Dusko Tadic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To tell you quite -- to tell you the truth, she was his great aunt.

utterances.speaker: MISS DE BERTODANO
utterances.text: Did you see Dusko Tadic before the conflict again after 2nd May?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it was then that I saw him and then I did not see him for a long time.

utterances.speaker: MISS DE BERTODANO
utterances.text: Do you remember approximately when you next saw him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it was in the month of June.

utterances.speaker: MISS DE BERTODANO
utterances.text: Where did you see him on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On that occasion I saw him because they were looking for him from Banja Luka. They were trying to find him, where was he, and he was not there. Then I heard he came from Banja Luka and ----

utterances.speaker: MISS DE BERTODANO
utterances.text: Where did you see him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I saw him, he came to get some of his things. He was looking for something. He met my son. Do you want me to tell you or?

utterances.speaker: MISS DE BERTODANO
utterances.text: Yes you tell us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He came across my son, when he came from Banja Luka, and he found some of his effects, some of his belongings, in his coffee bar and asked my son where could he store it, so as to keep what little he had found.

utterances.speaker: MISS DE BERTODANO
utterances.text: So Dusko asked your son where he could store some of his belongings from his coffee bar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, coffee bar, yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS DE BERTODANO
utterances.text: Where did Dusko store these things?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Then he stored them, those things of his with me. It was not much. Do you want me to tell you all what happened and what he brought?

utterances.speaker: MISS DE BERTODANO
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right. He first brought, but let me tell you, he brought a crate -- no, he brought a tool box with a car tool box. He brought a desk, some chairs that he found in his coffee bar and some tables from it. He also brought a hot water boiler and a thermal boiler or a part of the flush toilet, and then he had some clothes tied in a bundle, his children's clothes. What else could have been there? You know, three years, it has been three years now. I did not really think that I would have to remember those few things. It was not really much, nothing to write home about, but, well, you know, he wanted to store it and he did it with me.

utterances.speaker: MISS DE BERTODANO
utterances.text: So he brought them to you at your house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS DE BERTODANO
utterances.text: Was he on foot or did he come in a car or a vehicle?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, there was a truck, it was a closed, a covered truck. I think it was a medium sized truck, not big really.

utterances.speaker: MISS DE BERTODANO
utterances.text: What conversation did you have with him when he arrived at your house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, well, when he came I said: "Children, what are you doing? It is wartime. I am afraid", and he said, "Don't be afraid, that is all that I earned in my lifetime". That is what he said. "Do not be afraid, this is what I earned. I have got nothing left of the coffee bar. It has all been demolished".

utterances.speaker: MISS DE BERTODANO
utterances.text: Did you tell him that he could store it at your house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Why not, since this child brought it all, then why not, since he brought it?

utterances.speaker: MISS DE BERTODANO
utterances.text: Was he with anyone on this occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A driver, he was a driver.

utterances.speaker: MISS DE BERTODANO
utterances.text: He had a driver with him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A driver was with him.

utterances.speaker: MISS DE BERTODANO
utterances.text: Did you know this driver?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no, I did not. How could I?

utterances.speaker: MISS DE BERTODANO
utterances.text: How long did he stay at your house on this occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, he did not come in, 20 minutes, just to unload it all in the garage. That was that.

utterances.speaker: MISS DE BERTODANO
utterances.text: Did he talk to you at all about where he had been or what had happened to him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, nothing. They simply unloaded it all, turned and left -- nothing.

utterances.speaker: MISS DE BERTODANO
utterances.text: Have you seen Dusko Tadic since this time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Never again. I did not see him ever again since he was -- he escaped to Banja Luka, he left, he was gone, nor has anybody told me anything. No, I did not see him since.

utterances.speaker: MISS DE BERTODANO
utterances.text: Did anyone ever come to collect the belongings that he had left with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you how he came for his belongings, because he had nothing to live on in Banja Luka, so he was selling them, simply to make some use of them, to survive, because he fled to Banja Luka and you had to live on something. So, there was something, so -- and something he sent to mother because she had nothing to eat. So he sent this desk to his mother and the wash basin he sent to his mother and chairs and things like that from the coffee bar. He had to sell it in order to survive. So that is it. I do not know if I have told you all about it, but I think that is it. That is the story I know. So, you see?

utterances.speaker: MISS DE BERTODANO
utterances.text: But he never came in person to collect any of the belongings that he had left with you, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no, nothing. He never came because he escaped to Banja Luka and they were looking for him so he was hiding. How did he reach Belgrade, that I do not know. There it is.

utterances.speaker: MISS DE BERTODANO
utterances.text: Your Honour, that is a convenient moment.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: We will stand in recess for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: SAVA VOKIC, recalled. Examined by MISS DE BERTODANO, continued.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Miss de Bertodano?

utterances.speaker: MISS DE BERTODANO
utterances.text: Your Honour, in the event I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Is there any cross-examination, Mr. Niemann?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Madam, I think you said in your evidence that when Dule Tadic was in Banja Luka that people were looking for him, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is right. That is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Who was looking for him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the police and SUP were looking for him. They did not know where he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you know why they were looking for him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, they were looking simply to know whether he was still alive, where he was, because he had escaped to Banja Luka and they did not know where he was, where the children were, where their mother was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You said that he brought the goods to your house in a truck, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What colour was the truck?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it was not -- it was not a military truck. This was a private, a private lorry, a private truck, covered.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you remember the colour of it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would say some nondescript colour. It is difficult to remember. I know I saw a lorry, I saw a truck, and I was afraid. I said: "Jesus Christ, what is happening? We are at war" and so on. He said: "Don't worry. All I have is here in this truck".

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you saw him on that occasion, he told you that his cafe bar had been demolished, did he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He -- yes, of course. There was fighting. The drinks, everything valuable was taken away, the chairs and the tables. Then he brought only one table, one box of tools for car repair, the wash basin and the flush toilet. Then there was a -- there was a children's -- a set of children's clothing, textiles, in a sheet, in a bed sheet, and this was all tied and this was a bundle, for children.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: A moment ago when you were telling us about people looking for him, that was when he went to Banja Luka, Belgrade and then off finally to Germany, was it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know that they were looking for him. I know that he fled to Banja Luka. Now, you see, in our army he went to Banja Luka, how he lived there, but he sent a child, a son of his brother, who took some of the things from my garage to sell and to live. Later, we did not know where he was. Then we learned he had gone to Belgrade and later we had heard that he left for Germany. That is as far as I know. I do not know much more. I give you my word of honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you very much. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Miss de Bertodano?

utterances.speaker: MISS DE BERTODANO
utterances.text: Nothing arises, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Can I take off my headphones?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Not yet. Is there any objection to Mrs. Vokic being permanently excused?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: We have no objection, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Very good. Mrs. Vokic, you are permanently excused. You are free to leave at this time and return to your home. Thank you very much for coming.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I see you are trying to decide who will be handling the next witness. OK. Very good. Mr. Wladimiroff, you have won -- or lost. Would you call your next witness, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: I will, your Honour, it will be Dasic, Tomislav Dasic. TOMISLAV DASIC, called

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Sir, would you please take the oath that is being handed to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I shall speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Fine. Thank you. You may be seated. Mr. Wladimiroff?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Is your name Tomislav Dasic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: What is the date of your birth?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 19th October 1946.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Where were you born?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Daba, community of Sanski Most, Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: What is your nationality, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Where do you live?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: In which quarter of Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the city centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: What is your profession?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am a graduate agronomist and agricultural engineer. I also have a Masters degree, MSc, in agriculture.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Are you employed or self-employed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am the Director of the Prijedor Agricultural Station of the Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: What are your duties as a Director?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I run a state-owned enterprise, trying to implement scientific knowledge in agriculture. We also have an intermunicipal service, advisory service, extension service. We have experimental farms, two private pharmacies for pesticides and we try to improve agricultural production over four communities of Dubica, Novi, Kostajnica and the community of Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Is the type of your involvement working from your desk or are you travelling around for that purpose?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Both, both. I work in the field and in the office and I travel also.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Since when did you hold this position?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As soon as the war began I was appointed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: What was your profession before the war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was in the same agricultural service, and I was in charge of working in my field of speciality, because as my speciality is vegetables and actually I was working in five municipalities covered by our service.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Before the war you were travelling around too, were you not, in the area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Every day, practically every day, every day.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Do you know Dusko Tadic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know Dusko Tadic now. I met him in 1992. I had not known him before.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Could you indicate a month in 1992 when you first met with Dusko Tadic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Late September, early October perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Just in general how well did you since then know Dusko Tadic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I used to know him before from sight, but I knew his father, Ostoja. I worked in the field. I travelled a lot. I was on various commissions. I was the land evaluator, evaluator of the value of land. So I did not know him at that time, but I knew his father and although we had no contact I knew of him.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Is it fair to say that before the war you have seen him and since late September 1992 you got to know him better?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I was in his cafe on one occasion and I saw him there but, as I say, we had no direct contact.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Let us focus on the outbreak of the conflict. Do you know when the Serbs took over in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was on the eve of 1st May 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Do you remember the conflict broke out in Kozarac later on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Since I lived in the city centre, I learned only later that a soldier had been killed at Jakupovic between Omarska and Kozarac, that a soldier had been killed. The tank was ambushed and the Green Berets killed a Serbian soldier who was in the uniform of the Yugoslav Army. This was one of the direct causes which led to disagreement between the Serbs and the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: From there things got worse and Kozarac was attacked, is that true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The situation deteriorated and the rest, I do not know. I do not know exactly when Kozarac was attacked by the Serbian Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: While the conflict developed, let us say the period of the takeover in Prijedor and later on, did you continue to work or did you stay at home in that hectic period of time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After the takeover, we continued to work until Prijedor itself was attacked and actually I went to my job every day. Then after the attack on Prijedor, the situation became much worse and worst imaginable perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: You told us that you saw Dusko Tadic late September 1992, perhaps the beginning of October 1992, although you may have seen him on occasions before the conflict. What was the reason you saw him again late September, beginning October 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I met him officially in 1992 in late September, early October, because we were assigned to the same -- appointed to the same commission, to work together, and I was the chairman of that commission so I met him in this sense. Earlier, I had been to his cafe in March or April and I saw him then. I remember seeing him then. Later I learned that that was his, actually his restaurant, his cafe.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: What was this commission, what was the kind of work this commission was doing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This commission had the task of recording the situation in the field, the land, houses, deserted houses, deserted business premises, then the houses that had been vacated and that could be used by refugees, so that the refugees could be put into these houses if they were livable.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Was there a special reason in those days to have this committee organising these kinds of things? Were there a lot of refugees?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, at that time many refugees were arriving and there was no other reason but simply to accommodate the refugees. We had to find some places for them so they do not just live in schools or gymnasia and so on. Refugees came in great numbers, masses of people. They could not sleep in the park. There were not enough trailers, mobile homes. So we actually had officially to assign them to vacated flats so that we know who was where and where they could be housed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: This committee, was that an official committee of the local authorities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was an official committee of the local government of the Prijedor municipality to check the situation in the field, to record that situation and to submit the findings to the central municipal committee which was deciding as to who will be assigned what house, what apartment, what farm, so that these vacated buildings and vacated business premises could be assigned to other people. We were simply charged with recording the situation in the field such as it was, to make -- to take notes, make protocols, is there a building, what kind of a situation it is, if it is good enough for people to be housed there? So we actually were professional people making professional assessment. We had an agricultural specialist, then we had a geometer and Dusko, as representative of the local community of Serbian Kozarac. On the basis of our documents, on the basis of our protocols, the municipal commission later actually issued orders or entitlements to housing. While we, as a committee, as a commission, three-member commission, we signed the protocols and submitted the protocols to the central municipal commission, which was a legal body, a legally constituted body, to make property decisions in the municipality of Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: This committee, was that the only committee working in the opstina of Prijedor or were these committees organised on the basis of local communes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that time three such commissions were in operation. Before that there had been other commissions which had not been successful in performing the task. So, all three commissions when I was there actually were conducted by agronomists, agricultural engineers. We were people probably most serious and I, as the Director of my company, was actually sent on to that commission because I had enough experience and I knew that I could perform the job properly and I think to an extent we actually succeeded.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Which area did your commission cover?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My commission covered the area of the cadastral municipality of Kozarac, Trnopolje partly, Kozarusa, Kamicani, part of Dera, part of Bozici, to the right and left side of the main road Prijedor/Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: You also referred to a part of Trnopolje. Would that be the northern part of Trnopolje called Hrnici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was the part of Trnopolje up to Hrnici and we actually covered, also my commission was responsible for part of Hrnici as well, but winter came too soon and we did not manage to do that in that part.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Who were members of your commission besides yourself and Dusko Tadic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was Gordana Tadic, Gordana Sobot, a geometer. She was a member of the geodesics service of the Prijedor municipality. She had all the cadastral data, land books and things, and she actually knew who the owners were and she could take these documents in the field to decide whose building was where, who had what land, so that this was completely well organised on the spot.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Was Gordana Tadic related to Dusko Tadic or was she not; she just happens to have the same name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Her surname was not Tadic. She is married, Sobot.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Her maiden name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know the maiden name and she was not related to Dusko Tadic. I do not know the maiden name. She was married Sobot and now her married name is Sobot still.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: The transcript says there was Gordana Tadic, but apparently that is not correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no, that is not correct. Sobot, Sobot, because she was married but I cannot tell you the maiden name.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Thank you. When did your commission start to work or at least when did you start to work as President of that commission?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, we had some problems with the work of the commission because we had no car and we had no fuel. So that since I was very busy, it was not easy to organise this. We started probably in early October and then we worked intermittently since we had no fuel, no petrol, and actually I was very busy and I did not have enough time to work intensively. But later we managed to get the car. The municipality decided to allocate a car to us and so on. So when the conditions were better, we worked much more intensively and well.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: When did your committee cease to function?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, we worked until it was quite cold. We actually worked on our protocols outside in the open. We never entered any house. So probably between 1st and 15th December 1992, around that time, we stopped working, somewhere between 1st and 15th December. I do not remember the exact date, but I know that November was the time when we worked at full steam, so to speak.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: So you have been working, as I understand it now, from approximately 1st October up to 1st or 15th December?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right, right, some two to two and a half months altogether.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: What kind of involvement was required here? Would you be working with the commission once a week or twice a week or more?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, we sometimes worked for the whole week, four to five days a week, even on Saturdays, but this was a slow process because many people were not there. Many houses had been vacated. Sometimes it took us the whole day to finish one, one building, one site. Sometimes we could do three to four sites a day, depending on the weather when it began to rain, to snow. In late November the weather was very, very variable. It was like here in The Hague -- rain, sunshine and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: You told us that the Local Commune gave your commission a car, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the municipal authorities, not the local community but the municipal authorities, the executive committee of the Assembly of the municipality of Prijedor, they were deciding. They gave us an official car. Sometimes I was driving, but often we had a professional driver who was with us.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Would that professional driver take the car with him home back to Prijedor when your duties were finished at the end of the day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: That car belonged to the municipality of Prijedor, did it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Municipality of Prijedor. Though, in fact, on several occasions I used my own car for that purpose, because the municipal car was not available. So I used actually the car belonging to my company. Later, the municipality compensated us for the use of fuel. Since I was the municipal expert, they trusted me. They could use my car and then they later compensated us for the fuel and that was the compensation, because the agricultural station is also part of the municipal services, so that we could agree how to use this. In fact, even today we do not actually watch which car belongs to which institution. The important thing is that the task can be performed. Whenever we need, even now, to go into the field, we borrow the car from the institution that has a free car available.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Let us go back to 1992 again. When you were on duty inspecting houses, and if you used that car of the opstina of Prijedor or your car of your company, were you doing that job altogether, the whole commission, or were there mixed combination who would inspect those houses?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. We all went out in the full strength to each one of the houses, and some commissions failed in the work because they would not be complete. Three member commission always had to be there in its full strength, to be on the spot and investigate it, because we could not simply identify all those houses if we did not have a list and others; and the commission had three members, not two, and being the head of the commission, as a man who worked in commissions for years, simply never allowed this to happen. If all three of us could not go, then we would simply postpone going out into the field and leave it for another day.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
