utterances.text: So if you travelled by that car, all three of you would be in that car, would you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Was it possible for each of you to use that car without the others knowing that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Filing your observations, your inspection to the community of Prijedor, I take it that the community of Prijedor decided on the allocation of houses; you had only an advisory function, did you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We had a specific task and, as the head of this commission, we simply to take the stock of the situation in the field and it was up to them to set down the criteria for allocation, and I was not involved in this and, after all, this was none of my business. The thing was to take stock of the situation in the field, write a protocol, sign it and turn it over to the central municipal commission who then proceeded further and that was the end of our task. We were not interested in who would get the house, who got the house, who got a house and who would be -- they were being issued decisions to this effect, but they were all provisional.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, could you show this to the witness for identification, please? I think that will be 68, as far as I am informed. (Handed). Perhaps you could mark it as "A" because I will also provide later on the English translation. Mr. Dasic, this is a clean document. Have you ever seen such a document before?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Here, I have seen this document, this, but this is not a document that I had. I did not have it in my hands. I did not work with it. This is a document that was issued, from what I see here, for the use of housing, that is, of apartments rather than houses, private houses, houses standing on their own grounds or abandoned private property.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Could it be the case, Mr. Dasic, that this kind of document would have been used in town for apartments while you were using another document for houses on the countryside?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We had a different document on the spot -- we called it the protocol -- and its format was quite different, what we were supposed to register, to take note of when we went out into the field. The document which allocates abandoned property for use to someone was quite different. This is a somewhat modified document, I should say, of a somewhat more recent date.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Would the substance of the document be comparable to the documents you were using in your time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot hear very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Would the substance of the document be the same as the documents you were using in your time, the type of information contained in that document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The heading was similar, but the wording was quite different. It said house cadastre, cadastre plot, what part of it, auxiliary buildings, the size of plots of the property. This here is a description of an apartment, of a flat, of a flat in an apartment building, and ours had different wording, because we were talking about property abandoned in countryside.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Dasic, when you were doing this work with your commission on location, I take it that most of the time you were visiting empty houses, were you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is where we lost most of our time, and we -- as we went to empty houses to see which one of them met the minimum conditions so that some refugees could be accommodated there, so we would take stock of what was there in that house, so that is whether there was water, whether electricity was available, whether the roof was leaking or not and things like that. There were also houses which could be moved in, which had been moved in, and so we also, of course, noted down who had moved in, because the municipality had to issue certificates and to rule whether those people who had already moved in could stay in or that somebody else should go there. So we were to do that to begin with, whether the house was abandoned, whether there was a family, how many members and so on and so forth and, secondly, whether that was a livable house.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Would it make any difference for your work and advice you drafted whether the house belonged to an individual or to the State or to the community?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: These were all private property, abandoned private property. It was treated as abandoned properties since nobody lived there, nobody was living there, and the State, that is the municipality, was temporarily using it or, rather, allocating it for other people for use, to refugees, to use them. It was the decision of the government of the Republika Srpska to proclaim it abandoned property, which was then given upon temporary possession to refugees or of local person. I did not go into that, I do not know. But, be that as it may, it was a private property converted into State property and treated as State property, that is, at the disposal of the State, of the State authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: You referred to "local persons", would it also be the case that beside refugees also local persons who lost their house could be allocated such an empty house? Local people who lost their house because of the war or houses that were shelled in the area and, therefore, people were looking for other houses, applying to the government, to the local community, asking for another house? Was that a part of your work too, to inspect houses for that purpose?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not quite understand you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Inspecting empty houses for allocation to refugees, would that also implicate inspection of houses to be allocated to persons who lived in the local area but lost their houses because of the war, not being a refugee?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were to take the stock of the situation in the field and who that house would be allocated, that was not within our province as a commission. That was done by the central municipal commission. I simply was not interested. As a man, as a man who headed that commission, I was not interested in who they would give it to, to a refugee or to a person from that area, to a local individual or somebody who had come from Bihac or Jajce or Travnik. I did not go into that because that was not in the province of my work as the head of the commission or Dule Tadic and the whole commission which did this.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Am I right in thinking then that your commission had no power to give away any house whatsoever because those decisions were taken by the opstina Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We had no powers to do that. Our signature did not mean anything. Nobody could get a house on the strength of our signature. It was the municipal commission, headed with the President of the Executive Board of the commission, and the President of the wartime staff of the headquarters of the municipality of Prijedor, they had such powers. But, our commission which went out into the field, we did not have such powers and our signatures in that regard meant nothing, because I was not to allocate houses to anyone or to have any criteria of my own whom I should give them to. It was somebody else. We simply took stock of the situation in the field and then the commission knew who they were going to allocate it to. They had some criteria on the basis of which they looked into these cases and then allocated houses for temporary use for six months or a year or perhaps three months or five months. There were also such decisions, from what I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Could you please talk a little bit slower? It is much easier for the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Thank you. Am I right in thinking then that no one could just by his own decision occupy an empty house; you needed the permission of the opstina to do that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: People entered those houses on their own but, to make it legal, they had to obtain the paper, a certificate, a decision, from the municipal authorities or leave those houses so that they could be allocated to somebody else. Of course, people entered houses without asking anyone for permission, but some of them had to leave again because those who enjoyed priority, they had to be accommodated, and those who entered the house because they wanted to, who usurped such houses, they had to leave. There were such cases. He would see a house nearby and he would take possession of it, move into it. But, of course, that was always vacated and they had to leave and they could not stay in such houses, and there were so many people who had to be accommodated. There were children and they had to be put up somewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: In the former Yugoslavia, Mr. Dasic, was it not the system that, for example, large companies or large entities like hospitals, schools and those kinds of organisations had their own quota of houses they could give to their employees to live in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the municipality of Prijedor State companies had in 95 per cent of cases their flats, mostly flats in apartment buildings. As far as for houses, only the Omarska iron ore mine or rather the Ljubija mine, they had whole villages, settlements where they invested and helped their workers, their employees to build houses on their own grounds. At that time the municipality did not allow anyone to dispose of that abandoned property, but the municipality itself, they issued decisions and officially they were the ones who disposed of that property. I do not know if I was clear.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Wladimiroff, before you continue with that line of questioning.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: I forgot the time, your Honour, indeed.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: We will stand in recess and then we will proceed in closed session. So the witness then is excused until tomorrow at 10 a.m. We will then go into closed session.
